description: The Matlazihua ('woman who ensnares') is the female phantom of Oaxaca's Zapotec towns: a beautiful woman in a white dress with long loose hair who appears between one and three in the morning near rivers and empty streets. She lures drunken or lovelorn men into a trance and leads them into thorny thickets and ravines; some versions give her one foot, goat hooves, or a skeletal face.
source: Mexico Unexplained 'Matlazihua'; Multo Ghost 'La Matlalcihua'; El Universal Oaxaca
research_notes: Attested and well documented. The Zapotec/Matlazihua phantom (Nahuatl matlazihuatl, 'the ensnaring woman') haunts Miahuatlán, Sola de Vega and Talea de Castro, appears 1-3am near rivers and streets, and stalks drunks and lonely lovers. Recorded forms include a shape-shifter, a one-footed woman, a woman with goat/turkey feet, or a couple; early colonial writers linked her to Mictecacihuatl. The input's water-spirit framing fits her riverine appearances; habitat refined to Oaxaca's rivers and pueblos.

description: Chaac, the Maya rain god (Chaahk), is a humanoid deity with a long curling trunk-like nose, fangs and shell ear ornaments who hurls his lightning axe (K'awiil). He brings rain to the crops and dwells in clouds, mountains and cenotes; his four directional aspects wear red, white, black and yellow, and neglect provokes storms or drought.
source: Wikipedia 'Chaac'; The Met Museum 'Chaac Maya Rain God'
research_notes: Attested and well documented. Chaac/Chaahk is the lowland Maya thunder-and-rain deity with serpent nose, shell earrings and lightning axe; his bacab directional avatars (chacs) are painted red, white, black and yellow and stationed at the four world quarters. He corresponds to Aztec Tlaloc and is closely tied to cenotes and caves, matching the input's habitat. The record's amphibian associations (frogs, toads) are attested in Maya rain symbolism.

description: Chaahk, the Maya thunder-and-rain deity of lowland Guatemala, snorts rain through his long curling nose, wields a lightning axe and wears fangs and shell ear ornaments. He lives in clouds, mountain caves and cenotes and must be appeased with offerings, for his four colored directional aspects can unleash destructive storms or withhold the rain that the cornfields need.
source: Wikipedia 'Chaac'; The Met Museum 'Chaac Maya Rain God'
research_notes: Attested and well documented for the Maya lowlands including Petén, Guatemala. Same deity as the Mexico record; description varied to emphasize highland/lowland Guatemala usage, rain-bringing and drought/wrath behaviors, and cenote/cave habitat. The four directional bacabs with their colors are confirmed in colonial and modern sources.

description: In Maya belief the coyote is a nawal, a spirit companion and shape-shifting trickster of the forest's edge. K'iche' narrators tell how the coyote drums its ribs like a heart-beat to lure prey within reach, and its cunning marks it as a guardian of the boundary between village and wild, roaming the night world of caves, cenotes and the rain god's domain.
source: AIBR 'El coyote en la cultura maya'; Mexicolore coyote trickster
research_notes: Attested as a Maya nawal and trickster. The coyote appears in K'iche' and wider Mesoamerican lore as a clever animal-spirit; the 'coyote's heart-drum' tale (beating the ribs to lure prey with song) is documented. The input's elaborate forest-covenant narrative (diamond marking, glyph patterns, covenant with the forest) is unverified modern elaboration and was not reproduced; core nawal/trickster role and habitat retained.

description: Not independently attested as a Maya trickster or ancestral guide. No source records a crow spirit that escorts Maya families to Canada or turns snow into cornmeal; crows play no central role in Maya myth, and the nearest attested bird-demon is Vucub-Caquix, the boastful false-sun macaw of the Popol Vuh, defeated by the Hero Twins with a blowgun.
source: None — no independent source for a Maya crow; Popol Vuh Vucub-Caquix (Seven Macaw)
research_notes: Searches found no Maya crow trickster or diaspora-guiding crow. The record's description (white wing-markings like glyphs, snow-to-cornmeal, collecting stories) is modern invention. The nearest real Maya bird figure is Vucub-Caquix (Wuqub' Kaqix, 'Seven Macaw'), the bird-demon of the Popol Vuh who set himself up as false sun and was felled by the Hero Twins; noted as the correct analogue.

description: Not independently attested as a Maya trickster or guide. Crows are not major figures in Maya mythology, and the recorded story of a crow leading Maya families to Canada and turning snow to cornmeal is a modern fabrication. The closest attested bird being is Vucub-Caquix ('Seven Macaw'), the false sun of the Popol Vuh, shot down with a blowgun.
source: None — no independent source for a Maya crow; Popol Vuh Vucub-Caquix
research_notes: Same unattested figure as the Guatemala duplicate; the Mexico record repeats the identical fabricated diaspora narrative. No ethnography names a Maya crow trickster. Corrected analogue is Vucub-Caquix (Seven Macaw) of the Popol Vuh. Flagged as duplicate of crowmaya-guatemala; may warrant deduplication.

description: El Viejo del Monte, the 'Old Man of the Forest' (Kiwíkgolo in Miskito), is the ghost of a tireless hunter punished by becoming a shaggy giant with a single eye who now defends the animals of the Nicaraguan bush. He rules over deer and game, thunder and rain, and can ride as a monstrous horseman; hunters must ask his leave before taking any of his creatures.
source: Spanish Wikipedia 'Viejo del Monte'; Nicaraguan oral tradition
research_notes: Attested and well documented in Central American (Nicaragua, Costa Rica, Mexico) and Miskito tradition. The Viejo del Monte / Dueño del Monte is the spirit of an insatiable hunter transformed into a giant hairy, often one-eyed being (or a monstrous sabanero on horseback) who protects mountain animals, controls rain and wind, and can turn deer into jaguars. Input's 'tests travelers' kindness, grounding, healing' framing is thin but compatible; grounded and animal-friendship traits folded in.

description: In Yucatec Maya lore the owl (tunkuluchu) is death's messenger: its hooting near a home foretells a death, and it sings beside the dying. A famous legend explains this — after being humiliated at a noble's banquet, a proud bird was transformed into an owl, and it now cries out whenever someone is about to die, haunting ruins and dark places by night.
source: Yucatan Today 'Tunkuluchu'; Yucatec oral tradition
research_notes: Attested as the Maya death-omen owl Tunkuluchu; the banquet-revenge origin legend is recorded in Yucatec tradition. The input's 'water-spirit' framing, drowning power and possession abilities are NOT attested and were dropped; the owl's attested powers are prophetic crying and death omens. Habitat corrected from rivers/lakes to ruins and night haunts. Marked attested as the owl spirit, with caveats in notes.

description: The nagual (Nahuatl nāhualli) is a Mesoamerican shapeshifter bound to a person's animal spirit-double. Sorcerers and dreamers transform at night into jaguars, dogs, birds or other beasts; the Maya know the same being as way, written with a glyph of a jaguar-spotted spirit. Good or harmful, the nagual expresses a deep, lifelong link between a person and an animal guardian.
source: Wikipedia 'Nagual'; Houston & Stuart on Maya way glyphs; mayan.org
research_notes: Attested and well documented across Mesoamerica. Nahuatl nāhualli ('disguise, transformation'), Maya way (wayob, 'co-essence'), is both protective animal companion and feared shapeshifting sorcerer; jaguar, dog and bird are classic forms. The way-glyph of a jaguar-spotted being is confirmed (Houston & Stuart). Input's 'evil/dangerous' and 'guardian' duality both attested; refined to note the pan-Maya way concept.

description: Not independently attested as a Guatemalan water spirit. No source records a jungle river guardian named 'Wadlim' who keeps the fish and drowns offenders; searches surface only Maine surnames and place names. The nearest attested Maya and Central American water beings that punish disrespect for rivers include the Siguanaba and the guardian serpent-spirits of rivers and cenotes.
source: None — no independent source located
research_notes: Searches returned no figure named Wadlim in Guatemalan or Mesoamerican folklore; the name matches only Maine family/place records. Suggested real analogues: Siguanaba/Sihuanaba (water-side woman spirit) and Maya river/cenote serpent guardians. Marked unattested per policy; flagged for potential removal.

description: The Tupi-Guarani forest watchman is Curupira, guardian of the hunt: a red-haired, boy-like being with backward feet and a piercing whistle who defends trees and animals. He misleads hunters who take more than they need, making them lose their way in the deep woods, and punishes those who wound or fell without respect. He is Brazilian in origin, so the Mexico placement is an error.
source: Wikipedia 'Curupira'; Brazilian Tupi-Guarani folklore
research_notes: Attested as the Tupi-Guarani forest guardian Curupira: backward feet, red hair, whistling, punishes over-hunters and loggers by sending them astray (a liana wheel is a traditional counter-charm). The record's 'vigilant guardian with glowing eyes at forest paths' maps onto Curupira's sentinel role, but Mexico is a mislocation — the Tupi are indigenous to Brazil. Description corrected to Curupira and relocation noted.

description: The Olmec Dragon, reconstructed by archaeologist Karl Taube, is a composite water-and-earth deity blending caiman, eagle, jaguar, serpent and human features, with flame-like eyebrows and distinctive L-shaped or trough eyes. Carved at La Venta and San Lorenzo, it is among Mesoamerica's oldest dragon-like beings and foreshadows later Maya and central Mexican dragon and rain deities.
source: Karl Taube (1995) 'The Rainmakers', Mesoweb; Olmec studies
research_notes: Attested in Olmec iconography. Taube's 'Olmec dragon' is a composite caiman-centered supernaturate with eagle, jaguar, serpent and human traits, flame eyebrows, and L/trough eyes; it is associated with the watery earth and celestial realms and precedes later dragon gods. Input's generic 'water spirit' is expanded with Taube's specific composite traits and sites (La Venta, San Lorenzo).

description: Not independently attested: the inland Aztecs had no whale deity, and no such figure guards their lakes. The closest monsters are Cipactli, the primeval crocodilian sea-beast from whose body the earth was made (lured with Tezcatlipoca's severed foot), and Tlaltecuhtli, the ravenous earth-lady. Their lake guardians were water gods such as Tlaloc and Chalchiuhtlicue and the doglike Ahuizotl.
source: None for a whale god; Wikipedia 'Cipactli', 'Tlaltecuhtli', 'Ahuizotl'
research_notes: No whale deity exists in Aztec mythology; whales were unknown in the inland Valley of Mexico and play no role in the pantheon. Corrected analogues: Cipactli (earth made from its body; Tezcatlipoca lost a foot luring it), Tlaltecuhtli (earth monster demanding blood), and Ahuizotl (doglike lake water-spirit that drowns). 'Guardian of the lakes' maps to the latter rather than any whale. Marked unattested; flagged.

description: The Tupi water-woman is Iara (Uiara), a beautiful river siren with long dark hair who combs her tresses and sings on the bank, luring fishermen and bathers to drown in her depths. Colonists later blended her with the European White Lady, the Dama Branca, a pale figure in white seen near rivers and roads at night. She is Brazilian, so the Mexico placement is an error.
source: Wikipedia 'Iara (mythology)'; Câmara Cascudo, Dicionário do Folclore
research_notes: Attested as the Tupi-Guarani river siren Iara/Yara (Uiara, 'lady of the waters'): long-haired, beautiful, dwelling in rivers and seducing men to drown. The white dress is not core to Iara; that element comes from the European-influenced Dama Branca/White Lady ghost (documented by Cascudo). Description merges both while flagging the conflation; Mexico placement corrected to Brazil.

description: In Maya belief the jaguar is the great guardian of the underworld: each night the sun takes jaguar form to travel through Xibalba, the realm of the dead. Jaguar ancestor-spirits and protectors watch over lineage and territory, and rulers dressed in jaguar pelts and sat on jaguar thrones to claim this night power, as carved at Tikal, Palenque and Naranjo.
source: Lopes, 'Jaguar God of the Underworld'; Wikipedia 'Maya jaguar gods'
research_notes: Attested. The wildcat ancestor-spirit maps to the Maya jaguar: the Jaguar God of the Underworld (JGU), the night-sun traversing Xibalba, linked to lineage founders (Naranjo rulers impersonated it; Palenque Triad GIII). Jaguar ancestor-protectors and kingship symbolism (jaguar pelts, jaguar throne at Chichén Itzá) confirm the 'guardian of the undergrounds' role. Input's generic ancestor-spirit is grounded in JGU scholarship.

description: The Maya jaguar deity, the Jaguar God of the Underworld, is the night form of the sun prowling Xibalba with gleaming eyes and a spotted pelt, bearing fire and war onto incense burners and shields. In highland Guatemala the jaguar still guards caves and mountain shrines, and mountain lords are conceived as jaguars, tying the god to the earth and the deep.
source: Lopes, 'Jaguar God of the Underworld'; mayan.org Kinich Ahau; Tzotzil-Tzeltal ethnography
research_notes: Attested. The 'wildcat deity that embodies the mountain' corresponds to the Maya jaguar deity complex: JGU as underworld night-sun, God L with jaguar mantle and palace, and contemporary highland Tzotzil/Tzeltal beliefs where jaguars guard caves and mountains. The input's water-spirit archetype is adjusted: the jaguar deity is chiefly earth/underworld and fire rather than water. Habitat refined to caves and mountain shrines.

description: Not independently attested as an Aztec trickster. The Aztecs honored the jaguar and ocelot as warrior emblems, not tricksters, and their trickster roles belonged to the coyote. The nearest shape-shifting trickster god is Tezcatlipoca, whose nagual was a jaguar and whose smoking mirror worked mischief; no wildcat trickster figure appears in the sources.
source: None for a wildcat trickster; Mexicolore 'Why no bears in Aztec mythology'; Tezcatlipoca studies
research_notes: Searches found no Aztec jaguar/ocelot trickster. The ocelotl and jaguar were warrior-society and nagual figures (Tezcatlipoca's jaguar alter-ego); the coyote is the Mesoamerican trickster, and Tezcatlipoca is the shapeshifting trickster deity. Input's 'guardian of undergrounds' is unsupported for a trickster. Marked unattested; analogues noted in research_notes.

description: Not independently attested: the Kikuyu are a Kenyan people with no wolf ancestor-spirit, since wolves do not live in Kenya, and no such figure is recorded in Mexico either. Kikuyu belief centers on the creator Ngai and on animal characters such as the hyena in trickster tales. The record appears to confuse unrelated cultures and animals.
source: None — no independent source located
research_notes: Same misattribution confirmed in earlier batch (wolfancestorspiritkikuyu-myanmar): Kikuyu (Gĩkũyũ) are an East African people; no wolf ancestor-spirit exists in their lore, and the Mexico placement is doubly wrong. Closest real Kikuyu concepts: Ngai (creator), animal trickster tales (hyena). Marked unattested; flagged for removal.

description: No giant wolf appears in Aztec mythology. The attested wolf-like being is cuetlachtli, described in the Florentine Codex as a woolly, man-faced, wheezing stalker with a bushy tail, whose skin was worn by the 'Old Wolf' priest who tied captives to the gladiatorial stone of Xipe Totec. This is a ritual figure, not a giant.
source: Florentine Codex Bk 11; Wired Humanities 'cuetlachtli'; Seler; Mexicolore
research_notes: No 'wolf giant' exists in Aztec myth. The attested cuetlachtli (also glossed 'bear' by some) is a legendary woolly, man-faced, hissing stalker associated with Xipe Totec's gladiatorial sacrifice; the 'Old Wolf' (cuitlachueue) priest wept and howled while binding captives. Seler linked the creature with the sun alongside eagle and jaguar. The record's giant/swamp-guardian framing is unsupported; corrected to the ritual wolf-man.

description: Not independently attested as a Laotian forest spirit, and wolves are not native to Laos, where folklore features phi nature spirits, nagas and other beings rather than wolf deities. The same mislabeled record appeared in an earlier batch and is a modern fabrication; the Mexico placement compounds the error.
source: None — no independent source located
research_notes: Duplicate of the earlier wolfspiritlaotian-laos mislabel: Laos has no wolf folklore (no native wolves), and its spirits are phi, naga and animistic beings. The Mexico placement is also wrong. Marked unattested; flagged for removal.

description: Not independently attested: the Mapuche trickster is not a wolf but the fox, ngürü, cast in tales (epew) as a clever and sometimes diabolical 'ñiwa wentru' figure. Wolves do not feature as Mapuche tricksters, and the Mexico placement is mistaken, since the Mapuche live in Chile and Argentina. This duplicates a mislabel found in an earlier batch.
source: None for a wolf trickster; archivochile.com Mapuche epew analysis
research_notes: Confirmed unattested in batch 07 (wolftrickstermapuche-myanmar): the Mapuche trickster is the fox (ngürü), a 'ñiwa wentru' (devil-man) figure in epew tales; birds are used to represent human types. No wolf trickster exists in Mapuche tradition, and the record's Mexico placement is wrong. Marked unattested.

description: Not independently attested: wolves never lived in the Maya lowlands, and the Maya trickster and nawal is the coyote, not a wolf. No Maya story features a wolf trickster guarding the hills. The record misattributes a generic wolf-trickster template to the Maya.
source: None — no independent source located
research_notes: Wolves are absent from the Maya lowlands; the coyote is the attested Maya/K'iche' trickster and nawal (see coyotenaturespiritmaya-mexico). No wolf-trickster narrative exists in Maya sources. Marked unattested; flagged.

description: Not independently attested: no moon-bear deity with a white lunar coat, crescent pendant or role guiding the dead appears in Laotian folklore. Lao spirit lore centers on phi (nature spirits), nagas and protective village spirits rather than bear gods, and the recorded bear is a modern invention; the Mexico placement is an error.
source: None — no independent source located
research_notes: Searches found no Lao lunar or moon-bear deity; the elaborate input description (white moon-glow fur, crescent pendant, guiding the dead, fertility offerings of rice and coconut) is fabricated. Laotian supernatural beings are predominantly phi, naga, and village tutelary spirits. Bears figure in some regional (Hmong/Chinese) tales but not as a Lao deity. Marked unattested.

description: In Mixtec (Ñuu Dzaui) belief the ñuhu are sacred beings who guard places: ancient stones, caves and springs are their homes, and hunters, farmers and builders must ask their leave. Temple entrances were watched by carved guardians and by ancestral spirits with clawed hands who seize the disrespectful, as with Lady 9 Grass of the Temple of Death. The US location reflects the modern Mixtec diaspora.
source: Jansen & Pérez Jiménez, Ñuu Dzaui codices; Spanish Wikipedia 'Ñuhu'; Frassani, 'Pilgrimage and the temple of death'
research_notes: Attested as the Mixtec Ñuhu (sacred 'animated stone' beings who are lords/owners of places and must be asked permission to hunt, farm or build) and the ancestral guardians of temples and caves (Lady 9 Grass / Cihuacoatl as guardian of the Vehe Kihin, whose claws seize the disrespectful). The carved stone/jade guardian figures match the record's appearance. The USA location is a diaspora relocation, not the original Mixteca homeland.

description: The Three Sisters are the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) story of corn, beans and squash as three sisters who refuse to be parted. Grown together, the corn gives the beans a pole to climb, the beans feed the soil, and the squash's broad leaves shade it — a planting that nourishes and sustains life; if separated they weaken, and in one telling must be rescued from an evil captor.
source: Oneida Indian Nation 'The Three Sisters'; Haudenosaunee oral tradition
research_notes: Attested as the Haudenosaunee Three Sisters legend (corn/beans/squash companion planting). The three-sisters-maidens narrative and the values of mutual support are documented; the record's 'captured by evil forces if separated' detail matches versions where a sister is stolen and the others rescue her. Input's 'forest spirit' archetype is loose — these are agricultural culture-spirits, not forest spirits.

description: The Cherokee Thunder Beings (Aniyvdaqualosgi) are sky warriors who command thunder, lightning and life-giving rain and protect people from evil spirits. Though sometimes shown as giant birds, they are usually human in form, the children of Selu the corn mother; in some versions sons of the Great Buzzard, they shaped the mountains while the world was young.
source: native-languages.org Thunder Beings; Wikipedia 'Aniyvdaqualosgi'
research_notes: Attested as the Cherokee Thunder Beings (Aniyvdaqualosgi/Thunder Boys), a sky clan in human form distinct from the bird-form Thunderbird. The record's 'sons of the Great Buzzard who helped shape the mountains' matches recorded versions where they are children of Selu (corn mother) who shaped the landscape; they control storms and aid against evil. Attested; input confirmed with source detail.

description: The Cree Thunderers are great thunderbirds (Piyesiw): immense eagles whose wing-beats roll as thunder, whose flashing eyes strike lightning, and who fight the underwater serpents. They bring the rains of summer storms and are both feared and honored as messengers between the sky world and the earth; offerings are made to keep their goodwill.
source: Cree myths blog 'Wesakaychak and the Thunderbird'; native-languages.org Cree Thunderbird
research_notes: Attested as the Cree thunderbird/Thunderers (Piyesiw), giant birds whose wing-beats make thunder and whose eyes flash lightning, enemies of the underwater serpents (Mishipeshu in related Algonquian lore), bringers of rain. The record's messenger role between sky and earth is consistent with Cree cosmology. Habitat corrected to sky/storm rather than forest.

description: The Tlanuwa are giant Cherokee birds with feathers hard as metal, nesting on remote mountain cliffs where they carried off large prey, even whales in some tellings, and deflected arrows with their impenetrable plumage. Medicine men sought their feathers for power; only the great serpent Uktena could rival them, and the two were ancient enemies.
source: native-languages.org Tlanuwa; Archeology.uark.edu Cherokee Thunderbird/Tlanuwa
research_notes: Attested in Cherokee tradition: giant bird(s) with unbreakable metal-like feathers nesting on cliffs, arrows glanced off; carried off large animals (whales/people in some accounts); opposed the Uktena great serpent; medicine men obtained feathers. The record's storm-summoning behavior is a minor embellishment; core details confirmed. Habitat refined to remote mountain cliffs.

description: Not attested as a named figure: 'Transforming Beings' is a generic label, not a being in any specific tradition, and the recorded teaching role is a modern abstraction. Real Native North American shape-shifters include the Navajo skinwalker, the Athabaskan wechuge, the Algonquian wendigo, and trickster-transformers such as Coyote and Raven.
source: None for the label; comparative Native shapeshifter studies
research_notes: 'Transforming Beings' is a broad category, not an attested entity, and the input's description ('teach about transformation, healing, interconnectedness') is a generic New Age framing. Real attested shape-shifter traditions are listed as analogues: skinwalker (Navajo), wechuge (Athabaskan), wendigo (Algonquian), and trickster-transformers (Coyote, Raven). Marked unattested; flagged.

description: Saynday, 'Old Uncle' of the Kiowa, is the great trickster of the southern plains: a crafty old man who stole the sun to warm the world and outwitted famine, flood and enemies with his schemes. In 'Saynday and Smallpox' he was himself tricked, failing to halt the disease that swept his people — a tale of cleverness meeting its limit.
source: World History Encyclopedia 'Saynday'; Marriott & Rachlin, American Indian Mythology
research_notes: Attested as the Kiowa trickster Saynday ('Old Uncle'), a lazy, cunning old man whose exploits include bringing the sun, defying famine and smallpox ('How Saynday Got the Sun'; 'Saynday and Smallpox' where Smallpox outwits him). Input's 'helpful' trait fits the culture-hero side of Saynday. Habitat corrected to the southern plains rather than forest.

description: The tupilak is an avenging monster of Greenland Inuit tradition, assembled by a shaman from animal bones, corpse parts and other material and animated through song and ritual to destroy an enemy. It must return to land before dawn or dissolve into its parts; a stronger victim can turn it back on its maker, who is safe only by public confession.
source: Wikipedia 'Tupilaq'; Greenland Inuit ethnography
research_notes: Attested in Greenland Inuit (Kalaallit) tradition: the tupilak is a creature the angakkuq (shaman) fashions from parts of dead animals, corpses and earth, given life by incantations, and sent to kill; it dissolves at dawn if it has not returned to land, rebounds on the sender if the victim's magic is stronger, and public confession is the rescue. The Canada placement is approximate (Greenland Inuit; similar beings across Arctic).

description: Not attested as an ancestor-spirit or desert guardian in Diné (Navajo) belief. The desert tortoise (Ch'ééh digháhii) and mud turtle (Tsisteeł) do appear in Navajo symbolism — the turtle marks the center of the earth in the Tsidił stick game, and its shell signifies perseverance — but it is not a figure in the emergence story, and no guardian role is recorded.
source: None for an ancestor-spirit; NHMU Navajo baskets; nativehope.org Diné cosmology
research_notes: Turtles are not in the Diné emergence narrative and no 'turtle ancestor-spirit' is recorded. Real Navajo turtle motifs: Tsisteeł (Sonoran mud turtle) and Ch'ééh digháhii (desert tortoise) appear in symbolism — turtle as the center of the earth/universe in the Tsidił (stick) game, shell and turtle medicine used in ceremonies, shell as perseverance/protection. Description corrected to these attested uses; guardian/ancestor-spirit framing rejected.

description: Not attested: the turtle plays no part in Kwakwaka'wakw (Kwakiutl) animal-spirit tradition. Their ancestor and crest beings descend from mask-removing animals such as the Seagull, Sun, Grizzly Bear and Thunderbird, and their sea spirits include Kumugwe, Sisiutl and the fish-faced Pugwis. Sea turtles are absent from their coastal myth and art.
source: None for turtle; Wikipedia 'Kwakwakaʼwakw mythology'; U'mista Cultural Society
research_notes: Turtles are essentially absent from Kwakwaka'wakw myth and Northwest Coast iconography. Their origin/crest figures are the mask-removing animal ancestors (Seagull, Sun, Grizzly Bear, Thunderbird), and the nearest aquatic supernaturals are Kumugwe (undersea chief), Sisiutl (three-headed serpent) and Pugwis (fish-faced being) — none turtle-like. Marked unattested.

description: Not attested: the Choctaw record no turtle deity. Their emergence from Nanih Waiya, the Mother Mound, involves a cave and grasshoppers, and their water spirits are Okwa Naholo ('white people of the water') and the horned serpent Sinti lapitta. 'Turtle Island' appears in one recorded migration story only as a name for the continent.
source: None for a turtle deity; Wikipedia 'Choctaw mythology'; Mississippi Encyclopedia 'Nanih Waiya'
research_notes: The Choctaw pantheon and oral corpus (documented on Wikipedia and Mississippi Encyclopedia) contains no turtle deity. Emergence is from Nanih Waiya mound/cave with grasshopper episodes; water beings are Okwa Naholo and Sinti lapitta (horned serpent). 'Turtle Island' occurs only as a continental name in the Catlin-recorded migration account. Marked unattested; flagged.

description: Not attested: no turtle deity appears in Kwakwaka'wakw (Kwakiutl) mythology or among its mountain and sea guardians. Their supernaturals — Raven the creator, Thunderbird, Kumugwe the undersea chief, and Sisiutl the three-headed serpent — contain no turtle, and turtles are rare in Northwest Coast tradition.
source: None for a turtle deity; Wikipedia 'Kwakwakaʼwakw mythology'
research_notes: Duplicate of turtle-animal-spirit-of-kwakiutl: the Kwakwaka'wakw pantheon (Raven, Thunderbird/Tseiqami, Kumugwe, Sisiutl, Dzunukwa, Bakwas) has no turtle, and turtles are absent from Northwest Coast myth and art. The record's 'guardian of the mountains' and deity framing are unsupported. Marked unattested; flagged for deduplication.
